title: Unit mastery challenge
objectives: Demonstrate correct movement, capture, and blocking rules for every piece introduced in this unit

steps.text: Let's put it all together. This challenge mixes every piece you've met so far, on fresh positions — take your time on each move.

steps.prompt: Tap the g6 square — the g-file and 6th rank.

hints.text: Find the square where the g-file meets the 6th rank.
Here's the g-file and the 6th rank — find where they cross.
This is the square.
That square is g6 — file g, rank 6.

feedback.f6: Close, but that's f6 — one file to the left. Count again from a to g.
feedback.h6: Close, but that's h6 — one file to the right. Count again from a to g.
feedback.g5: Close, but that's g5 — one rank too low. Count again from 1 to 6.
feedback.g7: Close, but that's g7 — one rank too high. Count again from 1 to 6.
feedback.default: Not quite — count the files from the left first, then the ranks from the bottom.

steps.successExplanation: That's g6 — the g-file and the 6th rank cross exactly there.

steps.prompt: Move the rook in a straight line to any legal square.

hints.text: Move the rook in a straight line.
Any straight-line direction is fine.
Try this one.
The rook slides from b5 to b1.

feedback.default: Remember: the rook only moves in straight lines, never diagonally.

steps.successExplanation: That's a legal rook move — straight along the b-file, with nothing in the way.

steps.prompt: Capture the black pawn on d5 with your bishop.

hints.text: The bishop captures the way it moves — diagonally, landing on the enemy piece's square.
The pawn is one square diagonally from your bishop.
Move the bishop here to capture.
The bishop captures on d5 — one diagonal step from e4.

feedback.default: The bishop moves diagonally — slide it onto the pawn's square to capture.

steps.successExplanation: Bxd5 captures the pawn. The bishop moves diagonally from e4 to d5, landing exactly on the pawn's square.

steps.prompt: A bishop can move through its own pawn if there's no other legal way to reach its target.

feedback.default: No piece except the knight can move through another piece, friendly or enemy. If a bishop's own pawn blocks every diagonal, the bishop simply has no legal move that direction.

steps.successExplanation: Right — only the knight can jump over pieces. Every other piece, including the bishop, is blocked by anything in its path, friend or foe.

steps.prompt: Find any legal move for the knight.

hints.text: Knights move in an L-shape: two squares one way, one square to the side.
Any of the eight L-shaped landing squares works.
Try this one.
The knight can hop from c3 to d5 — two up, one across.

feedback.default: Knights move in an L-shape: two squares one way, one square to the side.

steps.successExplanation: That's a legal knight move — the L-shaped jump works no matter what's between the two squares.

steps.prompt: Capture the black pawn on f5 with your pawn.

hints.text: A pawn captures diagonally, one square ahead — never straight forward.
The black pawn is one square diagonally ahead of yours.
Capture here.
Your pawn captures on f5 — diagonally forward, one square.

feedback.default: A pawn captures diagonally, one square ahead — not straight forward.

steps.successExplanation: gxf5 captures the pawn. Pawns move straight but capture diagonally — this is the one case where that difference matters.

steps.prompt: Move the king one square in any direction.

hints.text: The king moves just one square, any direction.
Any neighboring square works.
Try this one.
The king steps from c5 to b5.

feedback.default: The king can only move one square at a time.

steps.successExplanation: That's a legal king move — one square, and the destination isn't attacked by anything.

feedback.0: A bishop is worth about 3 points — less than a rook's 5.
feedback.2: A pawn is worth about 1 point — the least of any piece.
feedback.3: Piece values differ a lot — a pawn (about 1) and a queen (about 9) aren't close.

steps.successExplanation: Right — a rook (about 5) is worth more than a bishop (about 3).

steps.summary: You've met every piece: how it moves, how it captures, and where it gets blocked — plus how to read any square by its file and rank, and roughly how much each piece is worth. Next up: the rules that govern the whole game — check, checkmate, and more.
